Brides' Chair

AreaAlgebraLogic
Game: Change the triangle and rebuild the squares on its three sides; this picture hides a surprising equality.
How to play: Drag A, B or C, or focus the picture, press 1 to 3 and use the arrow keys. Tick the boxes and slide the turn slider to see what stays the same.
Look for the math

Put a square on each side of a triangle and join the corners. The shape is called the Bride's Chair when the triangle has a right angle, but the surprises below work for every triangle.

The two little squares fill the big one

In a right triangle the square on the longest side has exactly the same area as the two squares on the other sides: AB² = AC² + BC² when the right angle is at C. Press "Make a right angle" to see it. This is the theorem the applet was built to show.

Three flanks of the same size

The triangles between the squares and the original triangle are called flanks. Move any corner: each flank keeps exactly the area of ABC, even though its shape changes. The logic test checks this on every triangle of a grid covering the drawing area.

A line with two jobs

The line from A to the middle of the far side of its flank is both a median of that flank and an altitude of ABC. It is perpendicular to BC and just half as long: AM_a = BC / 2. To see why, set the turn slider to 90°: the blue corner B′ lands on C, and CA cuts the new triangle B C C′ into two equal halves while AM_a becomes a line parallel to BC.

More hidden sums

The far sides of the three flanks satisfy A_cB_c² + B_aC_a² + A_bC_b² = 3(AB² + BC² + AC²), and the lines from the corners to the square centres meet at one point. The column also says that if A_cB_c is parallel to AB then AC = BC. All three claims were checked over the whole grid; none failed.

Try this: press "Make a right angle", set the slider to 90°, then tick "Show medians/altitudes" and watch B′ meet C.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
